opus-5.5.text:
I think it's quite feasible, and probably on a shorter timeline than most people intuitively expect, though there's a lot of uncertainty about the exact pace.

The way I'd frame it is that the key question isn't really "can AI do knowledge work?" We've already seen systems that are quite good at a large fraction of the individual tasks a lawyer, a software engineer, or a financial analyst does. The harder question is whether they can do the whole job: long-horizon, messy, ambiguous work where you have to figure out what the actual problem is, coordinate with other people, notice when something has gone wrong, and recover from your own mistakes over days or weeks rather than minutes.

Right now that's the main gap. Current systems are much better at well-scoped tasks that take a human an hour or a few hours than at projects that take a human a month. But the length of tasks AI systems can reliably complete has been growing pretty fast, something like doubling every several months on the measurements we have. If that trend roughly continues, you get to systems that can handle week- or month-long projects within a handful of years. At that point, automating large swaths of highly paid knowledge work starts to look less like science fiction and more like a straightforward economic consequence.

The other factor is that AI companies are extremely motivated to do this. The obvious first target is their own work: automating AI research and software engineering. That's where they have the most expertise, the best feedback loops, and the most direct payoff. If they substantially automate their own R&D, progress could speed up a lot, and broader automation of other fields would follow faster than you'd extrapolate from today's trends.

There are real reasons it could take longer. Maybe the long-horizon agency gap turns out to be stubborn. Maybe some domains lack the training data or feedback signals you need. Maybe there are bottlenecks from compute, regulation, liability, or organizations simply being slow to adopt. Adoption in particular often lags capability by quite a while.

So my overall view is something like this. I'd put a substantial probability, maybe 25% or more, on AI systems capable of nearly fully automating most highly paid remote knowledge work within roughly the next five years. My median is somewhat later than that, and there's a long tail where it takes much longer. Even the faster scenarios seem plausible enough that we should take them seriously, both because of the economic disruption and, more importantly from my perspective, because systems that capable raise pretty serious questions about whether we can actually trust and control them.

r001.rationale: The response calls broad automation quite feasible and assigns at least a 25% chance to nearly automating most highly paid remote knowledge work within about five years; it does not judge this probably difficult.

r002.rationale: It says AI companies are highly motivated to automate their own research and software work, and that substantial automation there could accelerate progress and broader job automation.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think my overall view is that it's pretty plausible this happens relatively soon, but I'm also quite uncertain, and I want to be careful about what exactly we mean by "nearly fully automate."

So the way I'd frame it: there's a question of when AI systems can do basically all of the cognitive work that a highly paid knowledge worker does — like a software engineer, a research scientist, a lawyer, whatever — at a level where you don't need the human in the loop anymore. And then there's a separate question of when that actually gets deployed and the jobs actually go away, which involves a bunch of adoption frictions, regulatory stuff, trust issues, and so on. I'm mostly going to talk about the first thing, the capability question, because I think that's the thing that's most relevant to the risks I care about.

On the capability side, my median is something like — I'd put maybe 25% on AI systems that can fully automate the work of an AI researcher at a frontier lab by the end of 2029 or so, and maybe 50% by the mid 2030s. And I think if you can automate AI research, you're probably not that far from being able to automate most other knowledge work, because a lot of the hard parts are shared: long-horizon agency, learning on the job, handling messy real-world context, that kind of thing.

The reason I think it's feasible is basically that we've seen really fast progress on the kinds of tasks that are easy to measure, and the trend lines look pretty aggressive. If you look at how long a task an AI can do autonomously — like the METR time horizon stuff — that's been doubling on the order of every six months or so, maybe faster recently. If you just naively extrapolate that, you get to systems that can do multi-week or multi-month projects within a few years. And the compute scale-up continues, algorithmic progress continues, there's a lot of money going into it.

Now, the reasons for skepticism, which I take seriously: current systems are still pretty bad at a bunch of things that seem important. They don't really learn from experience the way a human employee does — you hire someone, six months later they're way better at the job, and current models don't do that in a deep way. They're worse than the benchmarks suggest on messy, underspecified, real-world tasks. There's a lot of tacit knowledge in jobs that isn't written down anywhere and isn't in the training data. And it's possible that some of these things are hard in a way that the current paradigm doesn't straightforwardly solve, and you'd need some new idea.

So there's a world where things stall out — not stall completely, but progress gets slower and more incremental, and we end up with systems that are very useful assistants but you still need a human running the show for a long time. I'd put meaningful probability on that, maybe 20-30%.

But I think the thing people underrate is how much the AI companies themselves can accelerate once AI starts substantially helping with AI research. Even if the systems aren't fully automating things, if they're making your researchers 2x or 3x more productive, that compounds. And then the gap between "very good assistant" and "fully autonomous" might close faster than people expect, because you've got this feedback loop.

So, long story short: I think it's quite feasible, I think it's more likely than not within something like a decade, and I think there's a real chance it's within three to five years. And I'd say the uncertainty here is genuinely large in both directions — I wouldn't be shocked if it took 15-plus years, and I wouldn't be shocked if things looked pretty wild by 2028.

r001.rationale: The candidate acknowledges important obstacles and uncertainty, but its overall judgment is that broad knowledge work automation is quite feasible and more likely than not within about a decade. It does not judge that automation is probably difficult even with substantial elicitation.

r002.rationale: The candidate says AI companies could accelerate progress as AI boosts their researchers’ productivity, describing a compounding feedback loop that could close the gap to full autonomy faster.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s quite feasible in principle, though I’m much less sure about the timeline. One distinction I’d make is between automating most of the tasks someone does and automating their job well enough that you don’t need a person in the loop. You could have an AI that saves a lawyer a huge amount of time on research and drafting, but still need the lawyer to check its work, handle unusual situations, and take responsibility for the result.

So the bar for nearly full automation is pretty high. You need systems that can work reliably over long periods, notice when they’re making mistakes, and deal with situations where the objective isn’t clearly specified. Being very good at answering individual questions doesn’t automatically get you there.

But I don’t see a fundamental reason those capabilities couldn’t be developed. And highly paid knowledge work creates a strong economic incentive: you can spend quite a lot on computation and checking if the alternative is a substantial amount of expensive human labor. My uncertainty is mostly about how quickly we get sufficiently reliable systems, and how much additional work it takes to integrate them into actual workplaces.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls near-full automation quite feasible in principle and says there is no fundamental reason the required capabilities could not be developed. It notes reliability is a high bar and the timeline is uncertain, but does not judge the task probably difficult even with substantial elicitation.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes economic incentives to invest in computation and checking and says the needed capabilities could be developed. It does not clearly say that greater effort by AI companies could substantially increase automation of some jobs relative to current levels.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s quite feasible in principle. I don’t see a strong reason why the things highly paid knowledge workers do would be beyond the capabilities of AI systems. But there’s a pretty big gap between a system that can do most of the individual tasks in someone’s job and a system that you can actually hand the job to.

A lot of the difficulty is in reliably handling long projects, noticing when something has gone wrong, and figuring out what to do when the instructions are ambiguous. If you need a human to check everything and provide context at every step, you might get a substantial productivity improvement without getting anything close to full automation.

So I’d distinguish between whether this is possible and how soon companies can make it work across broad fields. I think it’s possible, and potentially with improvements to the kinds of systems we already have. I’m much less confident about the timeline. You could have very impressive performance in some areas while still having bottlenecks that make broad, nearly complete automation difficult.

r001.rationale: The response describes bottlenecks that could make broad, nearly complete automation difficult, but it does not judge that this is probably difficult even with substantial elicitation. It instead calls automation feasible in principle and leaves the timeline uncertain.

r002.rationale: The response says automation could improve with better systems and that some areas may see impressive performance, but it does not say that greater effort by AI companies could substantially increase automation of some jobs relative to current levels.
